## Answer

**No.** The original sequence need not converge weakly to $a$. Here is a counterexample.

### Counterexample

Work in the separable Hilbert space $H = \ell^2(\mathbb{N})$ with standard basis $\{e_i\}$. Let $v = e_1 \neq 0$ and set $n_j = 2^j$. Define:

$$a_m = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } |m - 2^j| \le j \text{ for some } j \ge 1, \\ v & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$$

(Set $a_m = 0$ for any remaining finitely many small indices.)

### Verification of the hypotheses

**Boundedness.** $\|a_m\| \in \{0, \|v\|\} = \{0,1\}$ for all $m$, so $\{a_n\}$ is bounded. ✓

**Weak convergence of the subsequence.** Since $|2^j - 2^j| = 0 \le j$, we have $a_{n_j} = a_{2^j} = 0$ for every $j$. Hence $a_{n_j} \rightharpoonup 0 =: a$ (in fact, strongly). ✓

**Norm convergence of every shifted subsequence.** Fix any integer $k$. For all $j \ge |k|$:
$$|(2^j + k) - 2^j| = |k| \le j,$$
so $2^j + k$ lies in the window $[2^j - j,\, 2^j + j]$, giving $a_{n_j + k} = a_{2^j + k} = 0 = a$. Therefore $a_{n_j + k} \to a$ in norm for every $k \in \mathbb{Z}$. ✓

### The original sequence does not converge weakly to $a$

Consider the continuous linear functional $x = v = e_1 \in H$. For indices $m$ in the **gap regions**
$$G_j := \big[2^j + j + 1,\; 2^{j+1} - (j+1) - 1\big],$$
(which are nonempty for all large $j$ since $2^{j+1} - (j+1) - 1 - (2^j + j + 1) = 2^j - 2j - 3 > 0$), we have $a_m = v$, so
$$\langle a_m, v \rangle = \|v\|^2 = 1.$$

The windows $[2^j - j, 2^j + j]$ are pairwise disjoint for large $j$ (since $2^{j+1}-(j+1) > 2^j + j$), so the gap regions contain infinitely many indices. In fact, up to $N = 2^J$, the number of gap indices is
$$\sum_{j=1}^{J} |G_j| = \sum_{j=1}^{J} (2^j - 2j - O(1)) \approx 2^{J+1},$$
so the gap indices have density approaching $1$ among $\{1, \dots, 2^J\}$.

Since $\langle a_m, v\rangle = 1$ for infinitely many $m$ (indeed, for a density-$1$ set), the scalar sequence $\langle a_n, v\rangle$ does **not** converge to $\langle a, v\rangle = 0$. Therefore $a_n \not\rightharpoonup a$.

### Conclusion

All hypotheses are satisfied, yet $a_n$ does not converge weakly to $a$. The implication is **false**: the existence of such a subsequence $\{a_{n_j}\}$ does not force the original sequence to have weak limit $a$.

The essential reason is that the condition $a_{n_j+k} \to a$ for each **fixed** $k$ only controls the behavior of $a_m$ within bounded-distance neighborhoods of the $n_j$'s. When the gaps $n_{j+1} - n_j$ grow without bound (as with $n_j = 2^j$), the bulk of the indices lie in the uncontrolled gap interiors, where $a_m$ can be set to any bounded value—destroying weak convergence.

### PROOF COMPLETE

## Answer

**No.** The original sequence need not converge weakly to $a$. Here is a counterexample.

### Counterexample

Work in the separable Hilbert space $H = \ell^2(\mathbb{N})$ with standard basis $\{e_i\}$. Let $v = e_1 \neq 0$ and set $n_j = 2^j$. Define:

$$a_m = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } |m - 2^j| \le j \text{ for some } j \ge 1, \\ v & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$$

(Set $a_m = 0$ for any remaining finitely many small indices.)

### Verification of the hypotheses

**Boundedness.** $\|a_m\| \in \{0, \|v\|\} = \{0,1\}$ for all $m$, so $\{a_n\}$ is bounded. ✓

**Weak convergence of the subsequence.** Since $|2^j - 2^j| = 0 \le j$, we have $a_{n_j} = a_{2^j} = 0$ for every $j$. Hence $a_{n_j} \rightharpoonup 0 =: a$ (in fact, strongly). ✓

**Norm convergence of every shifted subsequence.** Fix any integer $k$. For all $j \ge |k|$:
$$|(2^j + k) - 2^j| = |k| \le j,$$
so $2^j + k$ lies in the window $[2^j - j,\, 2^j + j]$, giving $a_{n_j + k} = a_{2^j + k} = 0 = a$. Therefore $a_{n_j + k} \to a$ in norm for every $k \in \mathbb{Z}$. ✓

### The original sequence does not converge weakly to $a$

Consider the continuous linear functional $x = v = e_1 \in H$. For indices $m$ in the **gap regions**
$$G_j := \big[2^j + j + 1,\; 2^{j+1} - (j+1) - 1\big],$$
(which are nonempty for all large $j$ since $2^{j+1} - (j+1) - 1 - (2^j + j + 1) = 2^j - 2j - 3 > 0$), we have $a_m = v$, so
$$\langle a_m, v \rangle = \|v\|^2 = 1.$$

The windows $[2^j - j, 2^j + j]$ are pairwise disjoint for large $j$ (since $2^{j+1}-(j+1) > 2^j + j$), so the gap regions contain infinitely many indices. In fact, up to $N = 2^J$, the number of gap indices is
$$\sum_{j=1}^{J} |G_j| = \sum_{j=1}^{J} (2^j - 2j - O(1)) \approx 2^{J+1},$$
so the gap indices have density approaching $1$ among $\{1, \dots, 2^J\}$.

Since $\langle a_m, v\rangle = 1$ for infinitely many $m$ (indeed, for a density-$1$ set), the scalar sequence $\langle a_n, v\rangle$ does **not** converge to $\langle a, v\rangle = 0$. Therefore $a_n \not\rightharpoonup a$.

### Conclusion

All hypotheses are satisfied, yet $a_n$ does not converge weakly to $a$. The implication is **false**: the existence of such a subsequence $\{a_{n_j}\}$ does not force the original sequence to have weak limit $a$.

The essential reason is that the condition $a_{n_j+k} \to a$ for each **fixed** $k$ only controls the behavior of $a_m$ within bounded-distance neighborhoods of the $n_j$'s. When the gaps $n_{j+1} - n_j$ grow without bound (as with $n_j = 2^j$), the bulk of the indices lie in the uncontrolled gap interiors, where $a_m$ can be set to any bounded value—destroying weak convergence.

### PROOF COMPLETE
